en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga,
Chapter on Forfeiture (Nissaggiyakaṇḍa)
The Chapter on Silk (Kosiyavagga), 13.
The Training Rule on Two Parts.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group of six monks, thinking,
“The Blessed One has prohibited having a rug made of pure black wool,” took a small amount of white [wool] for the border and had a rug made of pure black wool in exactly that same way.
Those monks who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and spread it about, saying:
"How can the group-of-six monks, having taken only a small amount of white [wool] at the edge, have a rug made entirely of pure black sheep’s wool?
Then those monks, having rebuked the group-of-six monks in many ways, reported this matter to the Blessed One... [and so on].
“Is it true, monks, that you have had a rug made from pure black wool by taking only a small amount of white wool for the border?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...

"How indeed, you foolish men, can you take only a small amount of white [wool] for the border and have a rug made from entirely pure black sheep’s wool? This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence... And thus, monks, you should recite this training rule: ‘If a monk has a rug made from entirely pure black sheep’s wool, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If he has it made with more than five parts black and one part white, that is an offense of wrong-doing.

If he has it made with more than three parts black and two parts white, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If he has it made with more than two parts black and three parts white, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If he has it made with more than one part black and four parts white, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If he has it made with less than five parts black and one part white, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If he has it made with less than three parts black and two parts white, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If he has it made with less than two parts black and three parts white, that is an offense of wrong-doing. If he has it made with less than one part black and four parts white, that is an offense of wrong-doing.’”
“Now, when a monk is having a new rug made, two parts of pure black wool must be taken, a third part of white wool, and a fourth part of brown wool.

If a monk should have a new rug made without taking two parts of pure black wool, a third part of white wool, and a fourth part of brown wool, it is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture. Regarding the term “new”: [it refers to a rug that has not been used for more than six years].
It is said with reference to the instrument of making.
What is called "spread" (santhata) is that which has been made by spreading [the wool], not woven.
"By one who is having it made" means either doing it oneself or causing it to be done.
"Two parts of pure black wool from sheep are to be taken."
Having weighed it, two scales must be taken up.
"A third for white ones" means a scale for white [robes].
"Regarding 'the fourth [part] of the variegated wool':
it is one *tula* of variegated wool.
If a bhikkhu takes two parts of pure black sheep’s wool, a third part of white, and a fourth part of variegated wool..."

If, without taking two equal measures of pure black wool, one makes or has made a new rug consisting of one measure of white wool and one measure of brown wool, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*) for the act of undertaking;
upon acquisition, it becomes subject to relinquishment (*nissaggiya*).
It must be relinquished to the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual.
And furthermore, monks, it should be forfeited in this way:

“… ‘Venerable sir, this rug of mine, having been made without taking [the prescribed amount], by having two measures of pure black wool and one measure of white wool and one measure of brown wool made, is to be forfeited.’”
“I relinquish this to the Saṅgha. … “One should give it” … “They should give it” … [and so on].
"I give it to the Venerable One.
If he completes what was begun by himself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If he has others complete what was begun by himself, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she has it completed by herself after it was begun by others, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she has it completed by others after it was begun by others, there is an offense of expiation involving forfeiture.
If she makes it or has it made for the sake of another, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If one obtains and uses what has been made by another, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
There is no offense if one makes it by taking half a *tula* of white [wool] and half a *tula* of brown wool.
Having taken a greater amount of white material and a greater amount of wool,
he makes it; or having taken pure white material and pure wool,
he makes it— a canopy, or a floor-covering, or a wall-screen, or a mattress, or a pillow.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The third training rule concerning two parts is concluded.
